stages.title: CCGT / utility gas generation
stages.summary: Combined-cycle gas turbines convert pipeline natural gas to electricity at roughly 60–64% LHV electrical efficiency—still the cheapest long-run kWh when you can secure the machine and the interconnect. Utility-scale plants sit offsite and feed the campus over HVAC or HVDC transmission. Lead times for large-frame turbines and interconnect queues often dominate schedule more than conversion efficiency.

stages.title: Turbine / genset (onsite)
stages.summary: Onsite gas turbines and diesel or gas gensets provide fast-start AC capacity inside or beside the campus fence. They trade fuel logistics for shorter interconnect waits and bridge peak, ramp, and maintenance cover. In this overview path they feed the shared site SST (same high-frequency node as offsite HVAC/HVDC landings), then land on the ~800 V DC bus.

stages.title: SOFC — solid oxide fuel cell
stages.summary: Solid oxide fuel cells reform natural gas on-site and produce DC electricity at high operating temperature (~800 °C for stationary stacks such as Bloom-class systems). They often win on time-to-power versus waiting for a utility interconnect: a month early on a 1 GW AI campus can matter more than small efficiency gaps. Native DC output aligns with 800 V hall architectures after a boost DC–DC stage.

stages.title: MCFC / PAFC fuel cells
stages.summary: Molten carbonate and phosphoric acid fuel cells are alternate onsite electrochemical paths, often discussed with combined heat and power (CHP) options. Electrical efficiency is typically lower than top SOFC claims, but CHP totals can be high where heat is usable. Like SOFC, they feed the shared DC–DC stage into the ~800 V bus in this overview—not the site SST used by AC generators.

stages.title: AC/AC step-up transformer
stages.summary: At the utility plant, an AC/AC step-up transformer raises generator voltage onto the high-voltage AC grid. Each transformer hop is roughly ~99.5% efficient. These are legacy low-frequency copper-steel units—the same product class behind the often-cited 2–5 year facility/grid transformer lead times—not the high-frequency SiC solid-state transformers used at the data-center perimeter.

stages.title: HVAC transmission
stages.summary: High-voltage AC carries power from the stepped-up plant bus toward the campus. Rough order-of-magnitude loss is ~5–8% per 1 000 km class; shorter hops are far smaller (transmission often ~98.5% per ~100 km class). At the campus, HVAC lands into the shared site SST that steps toward ~800 V DC—separate from the AC/AC step-up at the utility end.

stages.title: AC/DC converter (utility end)
stages.summary: For the HVDC path, an AC/DC converter station at the utility end turns high-voltage AC into high-voltage DC. Converter stations are expensive because they switch hundreds of kilovolts—a different product class from a data-center SST that lands at ~800 V. Rough budget: ~1% loss per converter station, plus the HVDC line losses downstream.

stages.title: HVDC transmission
stages.summary: High-voltage DC is the long-haul alternate to HVAC: roughly ~3.5% loss per 1 000 km on the line (after the utility-end AC/DC station). Buried HVDC can cost ~10× overhead on some corridors. In this overview, HVDC still merges into the same shared site SST as HVAC before the hall bus—do not confuse the utility converter station with that site SST.

stages.title: Site SST (solid-state transformer)
stages.summary: The shared high-frequency site SST is one node—not duplicated for HVAC vs HVDC. It takes medium-voltage AC (from offsite paths or onsite turbine/genset) and lands power toward ~800 V DC for the hall. SST products use SiC power devices and are scaling commercially through the late 2020s; they are distinct from legacy low-frequency copper-steel facility transformers (often 2–5 year lead times).

stages.title: DC–DC conversion (shared)
stages.summary: Fuel-cell stacks (SOFC, MCFC/PAFC) produce DC at voltages that usually need a boost converter before the hall bus. In this overview, SOFC and MCFC/PAFC share one DC–DC stage in the same column as Site SST—both paths then land on the same ~800 V DC bus. Collapsing redundant AC–DC hops here is part of why onsite DC generation pairs well with 800 V architectures.

stages.title: ~800 V DC bus
stages.summary: Once power is on an ~800 V (or ±400 V bipolar) DC busway, distribution looks more like industrial DC than classic branch-circuit AC. Busway and connectors move power across the hall (~99% class), then rack or blade 800→12 V LLC resonant converters (~97.5% class) feed multiphase VRMs. Collapsing the legacy UPS → PDU → PSU cascade cuts heat, parts count, and roughly ~5% conversion loss versus many AC–DC hops.

stages.title: Silicon — GPU / CPU hall load
stages.summary: The end of the chain: multiphase voltage regulator modules take 12 V (or intermediate rails) down to core voltages below 1 V at roughly ~90% class efficiency. Heat density at the package is a first-order cooling problem. Control and power silicon for VRMs and intermediate converters includes TI, ST, Infineon, and GaN specialists where those devices appear; the compute load itself is dominated by GPU/CPU silicon (e.g. NVIDIA-class accelerators in AI halls).

stages.summary: Rack or blade LLC resonant converters step the ~800 V (or ±400 V bipolar) hall bus down to ~12 V at roughly a 64:1 ratio and ~97.5% class efficiency. Power semiconductors (SiC/GaN where used) and magnetics dominate the bill of materials.

stages.title: Electrolyzer
stages.summary: Electrolysis typically consumes ~50–55 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen while the kilogram stores ~33 kWh of chemical energy (LHV convention)—about ~63% chemical efficiency in the annotated midpoint. That loss is paid before any fuel-cell conversion. Appropriate for stranded renewables or industrial feedstock paths; not a default AI hall baseload architecture.

stages.title: Hydrogen storage
stages.summary: Compressed or stored H₂ adds compression energy (~8% per 1 000 km class in the annotated model) plus leak (~0.04–0.24% per 1 000 km). Existing natural-gas pipes are not 100% H₂-ready (embrittlement); dedicated H₂ lines use lower-strength steels and ASME B31.12 practice. Storage η ~92% in the diagram is illustrative of those compression/leak costs.

stages.title: PEM fuel cell
stages.summary: Proton Exchange Membrane fuel cells use platinum and polymer membranes and require pure hydrogen. Electrical efficiency is often cited in the 40–60% band (~50% midpoint in the diagram). They fit vehicles, forklifts, and some backup niches—not multi-year AI baseload. Combined with electrolysis, round-trip often lands in the 25–35% band.

stages.title: Electric out (round-trip)
stages.summary: End of the electrolysis → H₂ → PEM chain: round-trip often ≈25–35%. Midpoint illustration: ~63% × ~92% × ~50% ≈ ~29%. Use H₂ for stranded renewables, seasonal shifting, ships/planes/trucks, or industry feedstock—not as a default wall-to-core path for continuous AI halls. Electrons on HVDC still beat molecules on physics for most point-to-point power moves.

stages.title: Cooling power path (CDU / liquid / facility thermal)
stages.summary: Heat removal scales with hall electrical capacity. Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs), liquid loops, facility chillers, and rear-door or direct-to-chip cooling sit beside the power path: every megawatt of IT load needs a matched thermal path. Cooling electrical draw (pumps, chillers, CDUs) is itself a power-budget line item as racks climb toward hundreds of kW.
